text: Chapter 3 covered role-based access control, least privilege, segregation of duties, access reviews, and privileged access as five distinct topics. This lesson assembles them into one connected model, and shows exactly which pieces would have stopped the Brightfield incident.

Role definitions start from job function, not from copying an existing person's access, each role's access written down and justified. Least-privilege mapping scopes each role to the minimum it needs, read-only where write isn't needed, row or column restrictions where full-table access isn't needed. Segregation-of-duties rules define which role combinations are never allowed on one person, checked before granting access, not after an audit finds the conflict.

A request and approval workflow means access isn't self-granted, a request names the role, a business justification, and an approver who isn't the requester. Periodic recertification, quarterly is common, has every active grant reviewed by a manager who confirms it's still needed, the step that catches access that should have been revoked but wasn't.

Brightfield's incident traced to exactly two missing pieces, no approval workflow requiring a scoped justification, and no recertification cadence that would have caught the still-active login. A role-based model alone wouldn't have been enough, RBAC defines what access looks like, but only approval and recertification catch access that was granted correctly and then outlived its reason to exist.

A model on paper isn't the same as one that's actually followed. Approval fatigue, a cumbersome multi-step sign-off gets rubber-stamped without reading. Recertification as a checkbox, a manager reviewing forty grants clicks approve all without genuinely checking. A model is only as strong as the discipline behind its weakest regularly-performed step.
Next up: privacy impact assessments, the last lesson in this course, and the process that catches these gaps before a system ever goes live.
